meaning: Doing something in accordance with rules, laws or tradition. Like “in accordance with” or “in line with”.
connection: Noun + にのっとって／にのっとり／にのっとった + noun

senses.label: Following rules
senses.meaning: Acting with laws, rules or procedures as the standard. Formal; common in writing and public statements. Stresses not straying from the set norms.
senses.connection: Noun (法律・規則・ルール・手続き) + にのっとって／にのっとり
examples: We will handle this properly, in accordance with the law.
In line with the competition rules, all athletes will be tested.

senses.label: Following tradition
senses.meaning: Doing something with tradition, custom or ancient ritual as the model. Common for ceremonies and festivals. Has the feel of “the old, proper way”.
senses.connection: Noun (伝統・古式・慣例・作法) + にのっとって／にのっとった + noun
examples: The ceremony was held solemnly according to ancient rites.
A festival true to local tradition was held again this year.

notes: 「則る（のっとる）」 sounds the same as 「乗っ取る（のっとる）」, meaning “to take over” or “to hijack”. Don't write it as 「乗っ取って」: 「会社を乗っ取る」 means “to seize a company”, which is a completely different meaning.
The particle must be 「に」: ✕「法律をのっとって」→ ○「法律にのっとって」.
The preceding word must be a norm such as a law, rule or tradition, never a person or data: ✕「先生にのっとって」→ ○「先生の指示に従って」; ✕「調査結果にのっとって」→ ○「調査結果に基づいて」.
The tone is solemn. Saying 「ルールにのっとって遊ぼう」 to friends sounds stiff, like bureaucratic talk; in conversation just say 「ルール通りに」 or 「ルールを守って」.

daily.title: Watching election news
daily.description: The news reports on how the election was run.
daily.example: The election was carried out fairly, in accordance with the law.

daily.title: At a Shinto wedding
daily.description: The officiant explains the ceremony to the guests.
daily.example: The Shinto ceremony will proceed according to ancient rites.

daily.title: Neighborhood sports day
daily.description: The referee reminds everyone to follow the rules.
daily.example: Let's play the game by the rules.

work.title: Handling a complaint
work.description: A customer service manager explains how the issue will be handled.
work.example: We will respond in accordance with our internal regulations.

work.title: Disciplinary notice
work.description: A company explains the basis for a disciplinary action in an internal notice.
work.example: In accordance with the work rules, strict disciplinary action will be taken.

etymology: 「のっとる」 is written 「則る」. It is thought to come from 「法（のり）＋取る」 (“take as the law”), meaning “take as a model or standard”.

similar.title: 〜に即して
similar.explanation: Both mean “in accordance with”. 「に即して」 stresses fitting the actual situation or facts and often follows 「現実・実態・事実」; 「にのっとって」 follows rules or tradition and stresses not departing from the established norm.

similar.title: 〜に基づいて
similar.explanation: 「に基づいて」 means using data, documents or experience as the basis, as in 「データに基づいて判断する」. 「にのっとって」 means acting with a rule or law as the yardstick; the preceding word is a “norm”, not “material”.

similar.title: 〜に沿って
similar.explanation: 「に沿って」 means going along with a policy, plan or wish, in a softer tone, as in 「ご要望に沿って」. 「にのっとって」 follows laws, rules or ancient rites, and is stricter and more formal.

formation: This is 「に」 plus the te-form of 「のっとる（則る）」. 「のっとる」 is generally thought to come from 「法（のり）＋取る」, “to take as the law”. 「に」 marks what is taken as the law, so 「Nにのっとる」 means “to take N as the standard”, which is also why the preceding word has to be a norm such as a rule or tradition. The te-form turns it into the manner of the next action, “doing it in accordance with…”; the continuative 「にのっとり」 is more written in tone, and 「にのっとった＋noun」 modifies a noun.

meaning: Forgiving or making an exception for someone out of regard for another person or a circumstance. Like “for the sake of” or “out of consideration for”.

senses.label: Pleading for someone
senses.meaning: Asking the listener to forgive someone out of regard for a person's standing or past merits. The second half is usually a request for forgiveness. 「私の顔に免じて」 is common.
senses.connection: Noun (顔・功績・〜さん) + に免じて + 許してください／ご容赦ください
examples: For my sake, please forgive him just this once.
In light of his many years of service, we ask for a lenient decision.

senses.label: Granting leniency
senses.meaning: The speaker forgives or relaxes a requirement out of regard for someone's sincerity or enthusiasm. Implies “this deserves a penalty, but I'll let it go”.
senses.connection: Noun (熱意・誠意・〜こと) + に免じて + 許す／大目に見る
examples: In view of his enthusiasm, I decided to extend the deadline by a day.
Since you were honest with me, I'll let it slide this time.

notes: Mind the direction: 「AにBを免じて」 means “forgiving B for A's sake”, where A is the person or thing being shown consideration, not the person being forgiven. ✕「彼に免じて許す」 (when you mean to forgive him) → ○「彼の誠意に免じて許す」.
It is not used for the cause of a good result: ✕「先生に免じて合格した」→ ○「先生のおかげで合格した」.

「私の顔に免じて」 is a way of pleading on someone's behalf, and it works only when the speaker really carries some weight with the listener. A junior saying it to a boss or client sounds presumptuous and rude; say 「どうか今回だけはお許しください」 instead.
The main clause is limited to expressions of pardon or leniency (「許す」「勘弁する」「大目に見る」「不問にする」); it cannot take punishments or ordinary actions.

daily.title: Making peace between friends
daily.description: Mediating between two friends who had a fight.
daily.example: For my sake, won't you two make up?

daily.title: A father apologizing for his child
daily.description: A child caused trouble, and the father apologizes to the neighbor.
daily.example: He's still just a child. Please forgive him, for my sake.

daily.title: Watching a period drama
daily.description: A character lets the other side save face.
daily.example: Out of respect for the boss, I'll back off for today.

work.title: A manager apologizing to a client
work.description: A subordinate made a mistake, and the manager asks the client personally for forgiveness.
work.example: Could you possibly forgive us this time, as a favor to me?

work.title: A veteran employee's mistake
work.description: Management discusses disciplining a senior employee.
work.example: In view of his past contributions, we decided not to discipline him.

etymology: 「免じる」 is the kanji 「免」 plus 「じる」. It originally meant “to exempt” someone from blame or duty. 「〜に免じて」 means “to waive punishment on the grounds of ...”, which led to “for the sake of ...”.

similar.title: 〜手前
similar.explanation: Both involve “face” or standing. 「手前」 is about your own face or position, so you “have to do it” or “can't bring yourself not to”; 「に免じて」 is about respecting someone else's face by “pardoning” or “making an allowance”.

similar.title: 〜おかげで
similar.explanation: Both credit someone or something for the outcome. 「おかげで」 means a good result obtained thanks to their help; 「に免じて」 specifically means being let off out of regard for their standing or merit.

formation: This is 「に」 plus the te-form of 「免じる」. 「免じる」 is a suru-type compound verb made of the kanji 「免」 and 「じる」, and originally means “to exempt (from blame or duty)”. 「に」 marks the reason or basis for the exemption, so 「Aに免じて」 means “letting it go on account of A”. Since the core idea is exemption, the main clause naturally expresses forgiveness or leniency; the preceding word is a favor, a merit or sincerity that makes the speaker willing to yield, hence the English “for the sake of…”.

meaning: The momentum of an action, or a sudden impulse, unexpectedly causes something else to happen.
connection: Verb ta-form／Noun + の + はずみで (はずみに)

senses.label: Momentum of an action
senses.meaning: The impact or force of an action unexpectedly leads to the result. The result is usually unexpected and unwanted. Like “with the force of ...” or “as I ...”.
senses.connection: Verb ta-form + はずみで／はずみに (転んだ・ぶつかった・立ち上がった)
examples: When I fell, my glasses went flying.
When the driver slammed on the brakes, luggage fell off the rack.

senses.label: On impulse
senses.meaning: 「ものの弾みで」 and 「何かのはずみで」 mean “on the spur of the moment” or “by some chance”, not on purpose. Often used to explain or excuse something.
senses.connection: ものの／何かの／その + はずみで
examples: In the heat of the moment, I said something really hurtful.
It seems something bumped the switch on.

notes: The verb must be in the ta-form: ✕「転ぶはずみで」→ ○「転んだはずみで」.
The main clause is an unintended, accidental result and cannot be something you did on purpose: ✕「転んだはずみで、友達に電話をかけた」.
「ものの弾みで言ってしまった」 explains that you didn't mean it, but saying only this when apologizing sounds like shifting the blame. In Japan, say 「申し訳ありませんでした」 first and explain afterwards.
「弾みがつく（to gain momentum）」 and 「弾みをつける」 are other uses of the noun, meaning “to pick up speed” or “to get fired up”. They do not express accidents and are not part of this grammar point.

daily.title: Telling family about a minor accident
daily.description: Explaining at home how you got hurt.
daily.example: I twisted my ankle when I bumped into a bicycle.

daily.title: Apologizing after a fight
daily.description: Telling your partner you didn't mean it.
daily.example: Sorry. I just said it in the heat of the moment.

daily.title: Dropping your phone
daily.description: Telling a friend how your phone broke.
daily.example: When I stood up, my phone fell out of my pocket.

work.title: Warehouse accident report
work.description: An employee explains what happened in an accident report.
work.example: When I pushed the cart, the goods fell to the floor.

work.title: Traffic accident news
work.description: The news reports on a car crash.
work.example: With the force of the collision, the car ran up onto the sidewalk.

etymology: 「はずみ」 is the noun form of the verb 「弾む（はずむ）」, “to bounce”. It came to mean “momentum” and “a chance impulse”.

similar.title: 〜拍子に
similar.explanation: The meanings are very close and often interchangeable. 「拍子に」 stresses “at the instant of…” and has a stronger sense of timing; 「はずみで」 stresses that the force of the action is the direct cause of the result. Also, 「ものの弾みで」 is a set phrase, and 「ものの拍子で」 is generally not said.

similar.title: 〜たとたん（に）
similar.explanation: 「たとたん」 only means “the moment…”, with no need for cause and effect between the two clauses; with 「はずみで」, the first clause must be what triggers the second, as in 「立ち上がったはずみで机が揺れた」.

formation: 「はずみ」 is the noun form of the continuative of the verb 「弾む」 (to bounce, to spring back), and originally means “the force of a bounce”. It follows the ta-form of a verb or 「noun＋の」 and means “the momentum produced as an action is completed”; the causal 「で」 (or the time-marking 「に」) then links it to the main clause. The whole thus reads “riding that momentum, something happened all at once”. Because this momentum arises incidentally and out of your control, the main clause is naturally an accidental, unintended result; extended to the mind, 「ものの弾み」 means “a moment's impulse” or “a chance turn of events”.

meaning: Pushing aside what (or who) should come first and focusing on something else instead.

senses.label: Neglecting what you should do
senses.meaning: Leaving what you are supposed to do and getting absorbed in something else. Critical or exasperated tone. Common as 「勉強はそっちのけで」 or 「仕事そっちのけで」.
senses.connection: Noun + はそっちのけで／そっちのけで + other action
examples: My little brother ignores his studies and plays games all the time.
He neglects his work and is obsessed with his fishing hobby.

senses.label: Ignoring someone
senses.meaning: Leaving out the person or thing that should be the center of attention. Common as 「本人そっちのけで」 or 「客をそっちのけにして」.
senses.connection: Noun (本人・主役・客) + そっちのけで／をそっちのけにして
examples: The parents are planning the wedding without even consulting the couple.
The clerks are chatting and ignoring the customers.

notes: The first part is the thing being pushed aside, not the thing you are keen on, and mixing them up reverses the meaning: 「勉強はそっちのけでゲームをする」 = doesn't study and just plays games; 「ゲームはそっちのけで勉強する」 = ignores games and focuses on studying.
It carries a clear tone of blame. Saying 「〜そっちのけで」 to a boss, client or elder is a direct criticism and very rude; used about yourself, it is self-mockery.
It is quite colloquial. In reports and official documents, use 「〜をよそに」「〜を差し置いて」 or 「〜を後回しにして」 instead.

daily.title: A mom complaining
daily.description: A mother vents to a friend.
daily.example: My kid ignores his homework and reads manga.

daily.title: A get-together
daily.description: Everyone got so caught up in talking that the food went cold.
daily.example: Everyone forgot about the food and got lost in conversation.

work.title: A meeting goes off track
work.description: A coworker complains afterwards that the meeting was a waste.
work.example: We ignored the actual agenda and just chatted.

work.title: News commentary
work.description: A commentator criticizes a city development plan.
work.example: The plan is being pushed ahead while residents' voices are ignored.

etymology: 「そっちのけ」 is 「そっち」 (“over there”) + 「のけ」, from 「退ける」 (“to move aside, remove”). Literally “push it over there”, that is, “set it aside”.

similar.title: 〜にかまけて
similar.explanation: Both mean “attending to one thing and neglecting another”, but they mark opposite things: 「にかまけて」 follows the thing you are absorbed in (「仕事にかまけて家庭を顧みない」), while 「そっちのけで」 follows the thing being neglected (「家庭はそっちのけで」).

similar.title: 〜をよそに
similar.explanation: 「をよそに」 mostly follows other people's worry, expectations or opposition and means “disregarding” them, in a more written tone; 「そっちのけで」 follows what should have been done or the person who should have been respected, is colloquial, and is more critical.

similar.title: 〜もかまわず
similar.explanation: 「もかまわず」 means not caring about surrounding eyes or circumstances, as in 「人目もかまわず泣く」; 「そっちのけで」 stresses putting the main task or main person aside to do something else.

formation: 「そっちのけ」 is made of 「そっち」 (over there) plus 「のけ」 (the continuative of 「退ける」 turned into a noun, meaning to move aside or exclude), so literally it is “shoved over there”. The thing set aside is marked with 「は」, which gives a contrastive “this I'll put aside for now”, and 「で」 then links to the other thing actually being done. The whole forms the structure “putting A aside and doing B”, which naturally carries a critical tone of “getting the priorities backwards”.

meaning: Written style. Something is completely impossible given the situation. Like “there is no way to ...”.
connection: Verb dictionary form + べくもない (する→すべくもない)

senses.label: No way to do it
senses.meaning: Circumstances make it impossible, even if you want to. Formal and stiff. Used with only a few verbs, like 「知る」 and 「望む」.
senses.connection: Verb dictionary form + べくもない (知るべくもない・望むべくもない)
examples: Back then, I had no way of knowing his true feelings.
On this salary, a condo in central Tokyo is out of the question.

senses.label: Beyond comparison
senses.meaning: 「比べるべくもない」 means the gap is so large there is no comparison. 「疑うべくもない」 means something is so clear it cannot be doubted.
senses.connection: 比べる／疑う + べくもない
examples: There's no comparison between a professional's performance and mine.
His talent is beyond doubt.

notes: Dropping 「もない」 reverses the meaning completely: 「調査すべく」 = in order to investigate; 「調査すべくもない」 = there is simply no way to investigate.
It does not mean “should not”: 「望むべくもない」 means “there is no way one can hope for it”, not “one should not hope”; 「疑うべくもない」 means “beyond doubt” (affirmative), not “doubt is forbidden”.
It combines only with a few verbs such as 「望む・知る・比べる・疑う・避ける」 and cannot be attached freely: ✕「行くべくもない」→ ○「行けるはずもない」「行きようがない」.
After 「する」, 「すべくもない」 is used. In everyday conversation it sounds bookish; in speech use 「〜ようがない」 or 「とても〜できない」.

daily.title: Reading a novel
daily.description: The narration at the end of a novel.
daily.example: What became of her after that, there is no way to know.

daily.title: Grumbling about housing prices
daily.description: A young person talks with a friend about buying a home.
daily.example: With my current income, owning a home is out of the question.

work.title: Industry analysis
work.description: A report compares the strength of two companies.
work.example: There is no comparison between the two companies' technical capabilities.

work.title: Historical research
work.description: A paper explains the limits caused by missing sources.
work.example: Now that the records have been lost, there is no way to know the truth.

etymology: 「べく」 is the continuative form of the classical auxiliary 「べし」 (possibility, obligation). Add emphatic 「も」 and negative 「ない」, and it literally means “there isn't even the possibility”.

similar.title: 〜ようがない
similar.explanation: Both mean “impossible to do”. 「ようがない」 is the general expression and stresses having no means; 「べくもない」 is literary and stresses that it is flatly impossible under the objective conditions, and only with a few verbs.

similar.title: 〜得る・〜得ない
similar.explanation: 「得ない」 stresses logical impossibility, as in 「あり得ない」; 「べくもない」 stresses that the objective conditions do not allow it, as in 「望むべくもない」.

similar.title: 〜とは比べものにならない
similar.explanation: Close in meaning to 「比べるべくもない」: both say the gap is huge. 「比べものにならない」 is used in speech and writing; 「比べるべくもない」 is more literary and stiffer.

similar.title: 〜べく
similar.explanation: They share a source: both come from the continuative of the classical auxiliary 「べし」. 「べく」 expresses purpose, “in order to…”; adding 「もない」 makes it “no way at all”, the opposite meaning.

formation: This is 「べく」＋「も」＋「ない」. 「べく」 is the continuative of the classical auxiliary 「べし」, which carries the sense “it is reasonable that one can; one ought to be able to”; 「も」 adds emphasis, “not even”; 「ない」 negates. Together: “there is not even the possibility one would reasonably have”. Since 「べし」 speaks of objective reasoning, 「べくもない」 expresses impossibility under objective conditions rather than lack of personal ability; and since it is a classical leftover, it is fixed to a few verbs like 「望む・知る・比べる」.

meaning: Used in laws, contracts and regulations to mean “shall ...” or “shall be deemed ...”.
connection: Verb dictionary form／ta-form／nai-form + ものとする

senses.label: Stating an obligation
senses.meaning: Sets out in a clause that a party must do something. Formal and impersonal, like “shall ...”. A typical contract and regulation expression.
senses.connection: Verb dictionary form + ものとする／ものとします
examples: Party B shall report to Party A by the end of each month.
Members shall pay the annual fee in advance.

senses.label: Deeming
senses.meaning: Treats a situation as a certain state: “shall be deemed ...”. Common in clauses like “no objection means consent”.
senses.connection: Verb ta-form／nai-form + ものとする／ものとみなす
examples: If no reply is received by the deadline, you shall be deemed to have agreed.
Anyone absent shall be deemed to have withdrawn.

senses.label: Assuming
senses.meaning: 「〜ものとして」 sets up a premise before discussing or handling something. Common in explanations, exercises and planning.
senses.connection: Verb (any form) + ものとして + 考える／計算する／扱う
examples: Calculate assuming there is no friction.
We prepared seats on the assumption that everyone would attend.

notes: When reading contracts, watch for clauses like 「〜しない場合は、〜したものとする／ものとみなす」: even if you say nothing, you are “deemed” to have agreed or renewed. Silence here does not mean refusal.
It cannot express the speaker's own decision: ✕「明日から毎朝走るものとする」 (in a diary) → ○「明日から毎朝走ることにする」.
This is the language of regulations. Saying 「お支払いいただくものとします」 to a customer face to face sounds like reading out terms and feels cold; say 「お支払いをお願いいたします」 instead.
「ta-form＋ものとする」 means “is deemed to have…”, while 「dictionary form＋ものとする」 means “shall…”, so changing the tense changes the meaning: 「同意するものとする」 = shall agree; 「同意したものとする」 = is deemed to have agreed.

daily.title: Reading a lease
daily.description: Reading the clauses carefully before signing.
daily.example: Upon moving out, the tenant shall restore the room to its original condition.

daily.title: Doing a physics problem
daily.description: The question gives an assumption.
daily.example: Assume there is no air resistance.

work.title: Drafting a contract
work.description: A legal officer writes contract clauses.
work.example: This agreement shall be renewed automatically upon expiration.

work.title: Writing company rules
work.description: HR issues rules on side jobs.
work.example: Employees who take on a side job shall notify the company in advance.

work.title: Event registration terms
work.description: The organizer explains the cancellation rules.
work.example: If we do not hear from you, you will be deemed to be attending.

etymology: Here 「もの」 means “the way things ought to be”, and 「とする」 means “to set as” or “to rule”. Together: “rule that it shall be so”. In legal texts it became the fixed way to state a provision.

similar.title: 〜ものとして (supposing)
similar.explanation: They share a source: both are 「もの＋と＋する」. 「ものとする」 is used in provisions and means “shall” or “is deemed”; 「ものとして」 is its continuative form and often means “supposing that…, and proceeding accordingly”, as in 「全員来るものとして準備する」.

similar.title: 〜たことにする・〜たことになる
similar.explanation: Close in meaning; both can mean “treating it as having been done”. 「たことにする」 is mostly colloquial and often means “let's just say…” in private (sometimes pretending); 「たものとする」 is the formal “deemed” of provisions.

similar.title: 〜を〜とする・〜を〜として
similar.explanation: Both use 「とする」 to mean “to set as” or “to regard as”. 「AをBとする」 designates noun A as B, as in 「合格点を六十点とする」; 「ものとする」 follows a verb clause and stipulates an action or state.

similar.title: 〜べきだ
similar.explanation: Both can express “should”. 「べきだ」 is a subjective judgment based on reason and carries the speaker's attitude; 「ものとする」 is an objective stipulation in rules, with no personal feeling.

formation: This is 「もの」＋「と」＋「する」. Here 「もの」 means “something that is as it should be” (related to the 「もの」 of 「〜ものだ」 for what is natural), 「と」 marks the content being determined, and 「する」 means “to set”. Together: “to set … as what is proper”, hence the obligation “shall…” in provisions. After the ta-form, what gets “set” is a completed state, so it becomes “deemed to have…”; in the continuative 「ものとして」, it means setting something down first and then proceeding, i.e. “supposing”.

meaning: Written style. An objective inference from the situation. Like “it is believed that ...” or “it appears that ...”.
connection: Verb／Adjective plain form, or Noun + である, + ものと思われる

senses.label: Objective inference
senses.meaning: Concluding from data or signs that something is probably the case. Objective and careful; avoids stating it as fact. Common in news, reports and papers.
senses.connection: Verb plain form + ものと思われる (〜たものと思われる・〜によるものと思われる)
examples: The fire is believed to have been caused by a carelessly discarded cigarette.
The culprit is believed to have entered through the back door.

senses.label: Cautious judgment
senses.meaning: A careful judgment about future developments or an evaluation. More formal and cautious than 「だろう」. Often 「〜ものと思われます」.
senses.connection: Verb dictionary form／Adjective + ものと思われます
examples: This trend is expected to continue.
This plan appears difficult to carry out.

notes: Here 「思われる」 is the spontaneous form, expressing the speaker's inference. It differs from the passive 「〜と思われている」 (“is thought by others to be…”): 「彼が犯人だものと思われる」 is ungrammatical, while 「彼が犯人だと思われている」 means he is regarded by everyone as the culprit, which is quite different.
It cannot be used for things you know for certain or for your own feelings: ✕「私はこの映画が好きなものと思われる」.
After a noun you cannot attach it directly: ✕「原因はたばこものと思われる」→ ○「原因はたばこによるものと思われる」「たばこであるものと思われる」.
In everyday talk with friends it sounds like a news broadcast or bureaucratic speech; in conversation use 「〜と思う」「〜みたい」 or 「〜だろう」.

daily.title: Watching the news
daily.description: The news reports the cause of an accident.
daily.example: The man is believed to have slipped by the river.

daily.title: Listening to the weather
daily.description: The announcer forecasts the typhoon's path.
daily.example: The typhoon is expected to make landfall in Kyushu tomorrow morning.

work.title: Failure investigation report
work.description: An engineer reports the cause to a client.
work.example: The defect appears to have been caused by deterioration of a part.

work.title: Writing a paper
work.description: A researcher analyzes the cause of a difference in the data.
work.example: This difference is likely due to the small sample size.

work.title: Market analysis
work.description: An analyst forecasts next year's sales.
work.example: Sales for next fiscal year are expected to remain flat.

etymology: 「もの」 is a formal noun summing up the situation. 「と思われる」 is the spontaneous form of 「思う」. Together: “(given the situation) it naturally comes to be thought that ...”.

similar.title: 〜とみられる
similar.explanation: Close in meaning; both are written-style objective inferences. 「とみられる」 is common in news and stresses an inference from observation or data; 「ものと思われる」 is used more widely in reports and official documents and is more cautious.

similar.title: 〜と考えられる
similar.explanation: Both express objective inference. 「と考えられる」 stresses a conclusion reached by reasoning and is common in papers; 「ものと思われる」 leans toward a judgment drawn from signs.

similar.title: 〜であろう
similar.explanation: Both are written-style conjecture. 「であろう」 is the speaker making a direct guess and can modify nouns; 「ものと思われる」 uses the spontaneous form to soften subjectivity, sounding more objective and careful.

similar.title: 〜とされる
similar.explanation: 「とされる」 expresses what is generally accepted or stated by an authority, not the speaker's own inference; 「ものと思われる」 is the inference of the speaker (or writer) himself.

formation: This is 「もの」＋「と」＋「思われる」. 「もの」 is a formal noun that sums up the preceding clause as “a state of affairs”; 「と」 introduces the content of the inference; 「思われる」 is the spontaneous form of 「思う」, meaning “one can't help thinking so”. Because of the spontaneous form, the inference reads not as “I subjectively think” but as “the natural conclusion from the circumstances”, so the tone is objective and careful, suited to news and reports. Wrapping the content in 「もの」 also makes the judgment sound steadier and less assertive.

meaning: Depending on how you look at or do something, the result can differ. Like “depending on how you ...”.
connection: Verb masu-stem + ようによっては

senses.label: Depending on your view
senses.meaning: From a different angle, things look different. Often with 「考える」, 「見る」 or 「取る」. The second half is usually an unusual evaluation.
senses.connection: 考え／見／取り + ようによっては
examples: Looked at another way, even failure is a good experience.
Seen from a certain angle, this painting also looks like a face.

senses.label: Depending on how you do it
senses.meaning: Different methods can lead to different results. Implies “done right, it's possible”.
senses.connection: やり／使い／言い + ようによっては
examples: Used the right way, this old tool can still come in handy.
If you phrase it well, you can turn someone down without hurting them.
Depending on how we play it, we can still win.

notes: It must follow the masu-stem: ✕「考えるようによっては」→ ○「考えようによっては」. It also cannot follow a noun directly: ✕「人ようによっては」→ ○「人によっては」.
The main clause means “it could also be seen this way” or “it might be…”, not an inevitable result: ✕「考えようによっては、失敗は必ず成功につながる」.
Saying 「考えようによっては、いい経験だよ」 to someone in the middle of misfortune can seem to belittle their pain, and is a tactless way to console in Japan; show sympathy first.

daily.title: Comforting a friend
daily.description: A friend is upset after finding out they were scammed.
daily.example: Look at it this way: it's good you noticed early.

daily.title: Sorting old stuff
daily.description: Cleaning your room and not wanting to throw out a box.
daily.example: Used the right way, this box is handy for storage too.

work.title: Business proposal
work.description: Reading data from a new angle in a meeting.
work.example: Looked at another way, this data could be called a new business opportunity.

work.title: Discussing costs
work.description: A project manager thinks there is room to improve.
work.example: If we go about it the right way, we should be able to cut costs further.

etymology: 「よう」 is written 「様」, “appearance” or “way”. 「によっては」 means “depending on”. Together: “depending on the way”.

similar.title: 〜によっては
similar.explanation: They share a source: both are 「によって＋は」. 「によっては」 follows a noun and means “in some cases”, as in 「人によっては」; 「ようによっては」 follows the masu-stem and stresses that the way of seeing or doing it makes a difference.

similar.title: 〜次第で
similar.explanation: Both say the result changes with the first part. 「次第で」 means the result depends entirely on it, as in 「努力次第で」; 「ようによっては」 stresses “if you do it another way, it might…”, and is softer.

similar.title: 〜いかんで（は）／〜いかんによっては
similar.explanation: Close in meaning; both mean “depending on how…”. 「いかんによっては」 is literary and follows nouns (「結果いかんによっては」); 「ようによっては」 follows the masu-stem and works in both speech and writing.

similar.title: 〜ようがない
similar.explanation: They share 「よう」 meaning “way, manner”. 「ようがない」 means “there is no way to…”; 「ようによっては」 means “depending on the way, it might…”.

formation: This is the masu-stem of a verb＋「よう（様: manner）」＋「によって」＋「は」. A masu-stem plus 「よう」 makes a noun, such as 「考えよう（way of thinking）」 or 「やりよう（way of doing）」; 「によって」 means “depending on”; and 「は」 is contrastive, singling out “some of those cases”. Together: “depending on the way, in some cases…”. Because 「は」 picks out only some cases, the main clause means “it might be” or “it can also be seen this way”, not a necessary result.

meaning: Taking advantage of a convenient situation to do something you shouldn't. Critical tone.
connection: Noun／Plain form + の + をいいことに

senses.label: Taking advantage
senses.meaning: Treating a situation as a chance to do something improper or selfish. The speaker disapproves. Like “taking advantage of ...”.
senses.connection: Noun (留守・不在・優しさ) + をいいことに
examples: Taking advantage of their parents being away, the kids made noise until late at night.
He takes advantage of his boss's kindness and is always late.

senses.label: With a clause
senses.meaning: When a whole situation comes before it, use 「のをいいことに」. The tone is just as critical.
senses.connection: Verb／Adjective plain form + のをいいことに
examples: Taking advantage of the fact that no one was watching, he threw trash on the street.
Since customers didn't complain, the store kept raising prices.

notes: Used about the other person, it directly accuses them of “taking advantage”. Saying 「私が何も言わないのをいいことに」 to a boss or client is a heavy complaint, to be avoided in business.
It is only for negative “taking advantage”; the neutral “using as an opportunity” cannot be expressed this way: ✕「先生の勧めをいいことに留学を決めた」→ ○「先生の勧めを機に留学を決めた」.
Without 「を」, 「〜いいことに」 means “luckily”, which is completely different: 「都合のいいことに雨がやんだ」 = luckily the rain stopped.
When it follows a clause, 「の」 is needed: ✕「誰も見ていないをいいことに」→ ○「誰も見ていないのをいいことに」.

daily.title: Complaining about a roommate
daily.description: Venting to a friend about a messy roommate.
daily.example: Since I never say anything, he's left the room a total mess.

daily.title: News about scams
daily.description: The news warns elderly people.
daily.example: Some businesses exploit older people's lack of knowledge to push expensive products on them.

daily.title: The family cat
daily.description: The owner finds the cat taking its chance to misbehave.
daily.example: While its owner was asleep, the cat jumped up onto the table.

work.title: Criticizing slacking
work.description: Coworkers talk among themselves.
work.example: Some employees are slacking off while the department head is away on business.

work.title: News on illegal business
work.description: The news reports on a company breaking the rules.
work.example: Taking advantage of lax regulations, it continued operating illegally.

etymology: 「いいこと」 literally means “a good thing”. 「〜をいいことに」 is “treating ... as a good thing (a good chance)”, which led to “taking advantage of”.

similar.title: 〜にかこつけて
similar.explanation: Both mean “using an opportunity to do what you want”, and both are critical. 「にかこつけて」 uses something as a pretext or excuse, as in 「出張にかこつけて観光する」; 「をいいことに」 exploits a situation favorable to oneself (others' leniency, their absence, etc.).

similar.title: 〜を機に
similar.explanation: Both can be rendered “taking advantage of…”. 「を機に」 is the neutral “using … as an occasion” and can describe positive things; 「をいいことに」 is only for exploiting a gap or doing what shouldn't be done, with strong criticism.

formation: This is 「を」＋「いいこと（a good thing, a convenience）」＋「に」, the same structure as 「AをBにする（to make A into B）」, literally “to take … as a good thing”. The first part (others' leniency, their absence, etc.) was never meant to be convenient for you, yet it is used as “a good thing for oneself”, and that is exactly “taking advantage”. So the main clause is mostly selfish or immoral behavior, and the pattern carries the speaker's criticism by nature.

meaning: Doing something despite illness, opposition or other obstacles, pushing through anyway.
connection: Noun (病・反対・無理, etc.) + を押して

senses.label: Despite illness
senses.meaning: Forcing yourself to do something even though you're unwell. Common as 「病を押して」 or 「体調不良を押して」. Often shows admiration or concern.
senses.connection: 病／病気／熱／けが + を押して + 出席する／出場する
examples: The president attended the ceremony despite being ill.
He played in the final despite his injury.

senses.label: Despite opposition
senses.meaning: Going ahead despite others' objections, warnings or difficulties. Common as 「反対を押して」 or 「無理を押して」.
senses.connection: 反対／無理／制止 + を押して
examples: Over her parents' objections, she decided to study abroad.
I knew it was a lot to ask, but when I asked anyway, they agreed.

notes: It is often used to praise or thank someone for “carrying on despite illness”, as in the speech phrase 「病を押してご出席いただき」. But you cannot ask others to do so: ✕「熱を押して来てください」 is very rude.
It follows only unfavorable conditions such as illness, opposition or hardship. 「背中を押して」 (“encouraging, giving a push”) and 「ボタンを押して」 (“press”) use 「押す」 literally and are completely different.
「を押して」 implies “forcing oneself, pushing through”, which differs from 「をものともせず」 (not minding hardship at all): ✕「彼は病気を押して、元気いっぱいに走った」 is contradictory.

daily.title: Sports news
daily.description: A report on the ace pitcher playing through injury.
daily.example: The ace took the mound despite the pain in his leg.

daily.title: Thanking a wedding guest
daily.description: The couple thanks a friend who came despite being sick.
daily.example: You came even though you had a cold. Thank you so much.

work.title: Political news
work.description: A report on a minister attending the Diet.
work.example: The minister attended the Diet session despite feeling unwell.

work.title: Thanking a client
work.description: Thanking someone for accepting a difficult request.
work.example: Thank you for handling the request, even though we knew it was a lot to ask.

etymology: 「押す」 originally means “to push, press”. It extended to “pushing forward against resistance”. 「〜を押して」 means “pushing ahead through difficulty”.

similar.title: 〜を顧みず／〜も顧みず
similar.explanation: Both mean “regardless of…”. 「を顧みず」 mostly follows danger, one's own safety or family, and means acting without a second thought, for praise or blame; 「を押して」 stresses overcoming illness or opposition and pressing on.

similar.title: 〜をものともせず
similar.explanation: Both mean doing something in spite of difficulty. 「をものともせず」 stresses not caring about the difficulty at all, looking brave and easy; 「を押して」 hints at strain and a price paid.

similar.title: 〜もかまわず
similar.explanation: 「もかまわず」 means not caring about others' eyes or circumstances and mostly carries criticism, as in 「人目もかまわず」; 「を押して」 usually carries sympathy or admiration.

formation: This is 「を」 plus the te-form of 「押す」. 「押す」 originally means “to push, to press”, so 「〜を押す」 is “to hold down or push aside …”. If you see illness, opposition or hardship as resistance standing in the way, 「を押して」 means “pressing down the resistance and going forward”. Because it is forced through by pushing, it implies strain and a price paid, and the speaker often feels admiration or worry; the te-form makes it the premise state of the main action.

meaning: Taking facts, experience or opinions as a basis, and then thinking or acting further.
connection: Noun + を踏まえて／を踏まえ／を踏まえた + noun

senses.label: Based on
senses.meaning: Treats facts or results as the premise for judgment and considers the next step. Common in meetings and reports. Like “based on” or “in light of”.
senses.connection: Noun (結果・現状・経験・反省) + を踏まえて／を踏まえ + 検討する／判断する
examples: I'd like to decide on our future direction based on the survey results.
Learning from last time, we started preparing earlier this time.

senses.label: Modifying a noun
senses.meaning: 「〜を踏まえた + noun」 means “... grounded in ...”, modifying proposals, measures or plans.
senses.connection: Noun + を踏まえた + noun (提案・対策・議論)
examples: Measures that reflect the views of front-line staff are needed.
A revision reflecting the experts' comments has been drawn up.

notes: The particle is 「を」, not 「に」: ✕「調査結果に踏まえて」→ ○「調査結果を踏まえて」 (easily confused with 「に基づいて」).
The verb is 「踏まえる」, not 「踏む」: ✕「結果を踏んで」.
The first part is a fact, experience or opinion that already exists; it does not take future matters: ✕「来年の計画を踏まえて」 (if the plan is not yet decided).
In Japanese business, 「ご意見を踏まえて検討いたします」 is often a polite way of holding back: it only means “we'll take it into account”, not a promise to adopt it.

daily.title: Political news
daily.description: The news reports what the government's decision is based on.
daily.example: The government will decide on easing restrictions in light of the infection situation.

daily.title: Adjusting a study plan
daily.description: A student revises their plan after a mock exam.
daily.example: Based on my mock exam results, I redid my study plan.

work.title: Wrapping up a meeting
work.description: The person in charge speaks at the end of the meeting.
work.example: Taking today's feedback into account, we will submit a new proposal.

work.title: Drawing up a budget
work.description: The finance department explains the basis for the budget.
work.example: We prepared a draft budget based on last year's results.

work.title: Writing a paper
work.description: How to write the introduction of a paper.
work.example: Building on previous research, this section sets out the issues addressed in this study.

etymology: 「踏まえる」 shares its root with 「踏む」 (“to step on”). It originally meant “to stand firmly with your feet”, and came to mean “to take ... as your footing”.

similar.title: 〜に基づいて
similar.explanation: Both mean “on the basis of…”. 「に基づいて」 uses data or rules as the direct basis and follows them; 「を踏まえて」 takes the first part as a premise and thinks further from there, stressing “taking into account”.

similar.title: 〜をもとに(して)
similar.explanation: 「をもとに」 means creating or concluding from material, as in 「実話をもとにした映画」; 「を踏まえて」 stresses using facts and experience as the premise for judging the next step.

similar.title: 〜を前提に／〜を前提として
similar.explanation: Both carry “on the premise of…”. The first part of 「を前提に」 is often an assumed or agreed condition, as in 「結婚を前提に」; the first part of 「を踏まえて」 is an established fact.

formation: This is 「を」 plus the te-form of 「踏まえる」. 「踏まえる」 shares its origin with 「踏む（to step on）」 and originally means “to plant one's feet firmly”. 「〜を踏まえて」 is “first stand firmly on the first part, then take a step forward”. So the first part must be a fact, experience or opinion that already exists and can be “stood on”, and the main clause is a judgment or action built on it. 「を踏まえた＋noun」 means “based on…”.

meaning: 「をもってすれば」 means that with a certain ability or means, something can be achieved. 「をもってしても」 means that even with it, it cannot.
connection: Noun + をもってすれば／をもってしても

senses.label: With ... , it's possible
senses.meaning: With the outstanding ability or means before it, something difficult can be achieved. Shows high regard for that ability. The second half is often 「できる」, 「可能だ」 or 「だろう」.
senses.connection: Noun (実力・技術・才能) + をもってすれば
examples: With his ability, winning the championship is not just a dream.
With modern medicine, this disease can be cured.

senses.label: Even with ...
senses.meaning: Even with such great ability or means, it cannot be done. Stresses how hard it is. The second half is usually negative or 「難しい」.
senses.connection: Noun + をもってしても + 〜ない／難しい
examples: Even with the latest technology, predicting earthquakes is difficult.
Even he, who was called a genius, couldn't solve this problem.

notes: 「すれば」 and 「しても」 differ by one syllable and mean opposite things: 「彼の力をもってすれば解ける」 = with his ability it can be solved; 「彼の力をもってしても解けない」 = even with his ability it cannot be solved.
The first part is a highly regarded ability or means. Saying 「私の実力をもってすれば」 about yourself sounds very arrogant and is best avoided in Japan.
After 「をもってしても」 you need a negative or something like 「難しい」: ✕「最新技術をもってしても、成功した」.
It cannot take negative or ordinary things: ✕「彼の下手な腕をもってすれば」.

daily.title: Sports news
daily.description: A commentator praises an athlete's speed.
daily.example: With his speed, breaking the record is possible.

daily.title: Reading popular science
daily.description: A book talks about the mysteries of the universe.
daily.example: Even with modern science, the universe still holds many mysteries.

work.title: Business talks
work.description: Expressing confidence in a partner company.
work.example: We are confident that with your company's technical expertise, this can certainly be achieved.

work.title: Economic news
work.description: Commenting on the effect of measures against rising prices.
work.example: Even with the government's measures, prices kept rising.

etymology: 「もって」 is the sound-changed 「持って」 from 「持ちて」. In kanbun reading it is written 「以て」, meaning “with, by means of”. Adding 「すれば／しても」 made a set pattern for condition and concession.

similar.title: 〜をもって
similar.explanation: They share a source. 「をもって」 simply expresses means or a time limit, as in 「書面をもって」「本日をもって」; adding 「すれば／しても」 makes a conditional or concessive and implies high regard for the first part.

similar.title: 〜にかかったら／〜にかかっては
similar.explanation: Close in meaning; both mean “once it's in someone's hands…”. 「にかかったら」 is colloquial, mostly follows people, and is often a bit teasing; 「をもってすれば」 is literary and mostly follows abilities or technology.

similar.title: 〜としても
similar.explanation: Both are concessive. 「としても」 is the general “even if…”; 「をもってしても」 stresses that even a powerful means fails, highlighting how hard the matter is.

formation: This is 「をもって」＋ the conditional 「すれば」 or concessive 「しても」 of 「する」. 「をもって」 comes from 「持って」 and is written 「以て」 in kanbun reading, meaning “with, by means of”; 「する」 here means “to do it with that”. So 「〜をもってすれば」 = “if one does it with … (it can be done)”, and 「〜をもってしても」 = “even if one does it with … (it can't be done)”. Since the whole structure takes the first part as a means, it must be an ability or technique, usually a strong and admirable one, and the concessive form uses it to set off how hard the matter is.

meaning: Written style. “Even without doing ...”: it's fine not to do it, or the result holds anyway.
connection: Verb nai-form (drop ない) + ずとも (する→せずとも)

senses.label: No need to
senses.meaning: It's fine not to do it. The second half is usually 「よい」, 「構わない」 or 「分かる」. A written version of 「〜なくても」.
senses.connection: Verb nai-stem + ずともよい／ずとも分かる
examples: There's no need to hurry like that.
You don't have to say it. I know how you feel.

senses.label: Even without
senses.meaning: Even without the condition, the result still holds. Has the sense that “it's naturally so”.
senses.connection: Verb nai-stem／Noun + なら + ずとも + result
examples: Even a non-expert can probably see this painting's value.
Even without a dictionary, you can guess the meaning from context.

notes: The form is the nai-stem without 「ない」: ✕「行かないずとも」→ ○「行かずとも」; 「する」 becomes 「せずとも」, not ✕「しずとも」.
Don't confuse it with 「ずして」: 「戦わずして勝つ」 is “to win without fighting” (sequential), while 「戦わずとも勝てる」 is “can win even without fighting” (concessive).
「〜ずともよい」 sounds archaic and talks down to the listener. Saying 「来ずともよい」 to a boss or client is condescending; say 「お越しいただかなくても大丈夫です」 instead.
「言わずと知れた（well known）」 is an idiom and is not 「ずとも」.

daily.title: Watching a period drama
daily.description: An old samurai reassures a young man.
daily.example: You need not worry. Leave it to me.

daily.title: An elder to a youngster
daily.description: A grandfather speaks to his grandson, who came to say thanks.
daily.example: There's no need to thank me.

work.title: Event notice
work.description: The organizer explains how to join in a notice.
work.example: You can join on the day without registering in advance.

work.title: Opinion column
work.description: A commentator thinks the result is obvious.
work.example: Even without looking at the numbers, the result is clear.

etymology: Made from the classical negative auxiliary 「ず」 plus the concessive conjunctive particle 「とも」. It corresponds to modern 「〜なくても」.

similar.title: 〜なくてもいい
similar.explanation: Same meaning: 「ずともよい」 is the literary, archaic way of saying 「なくてもいい」. In daily conversation use 「なくてもいい」.

similar.title: 〜までもない・〜までもなく
similar.explanation: Both can mean “no need to…”. 「までもない」 stresses that it is simple or obvious and there is no need to go that far, as in 「言うまでもない」; 「ずとも」 is the general “even without…”, as in 「言わずとも分かる」.

similar.title: 〜とも (even if)
similar.explanation: They share a source. 「とも」 is the classical concessive “even if…”, following the adjective ku-form or the volitional; 「ずとも」 is the form where it follows the negative auxiliary 「ず」.

similar.title: 〜ずして
similar.explanation: Both are built on the negative 「ず」. 「ずして」 means “reaching … without doing” and is sequential, as in 「戦わずして勝つ」; 「ずとも」 is concessive, “even without doing”.

formation: This is the classical negative auxiliary 「ず」 plus the concessive particle 「とも」, equivalent to the modern 「〜なくても」. 「ず」 negates the action and 「とも」 means “even if”, so together: “even if one doesn't do…”. Before 「よい・構わない」 it means “it's fine even if you don't”, i.e. “no need to”; before a general statement it means “even without the first part, the second still holds”. Since both parts are classical, the whole has a literary, archaic color.

meaning: Written style. A concessive condition, “even if ...”, attaching to the ku-form of i-adjectives, the volitional form of verbs and so on.
connection: i-adjective ku-form／Verb volitional form + とも

senses.label: Adjective + とも
senses.meaning: Even in that state, the result does not change. A written version of 「〜くても」. Often paired with 「たとえ」 or 「どんなに」.
senses.connection: i-adjective ku-form + とも (苦しくとも・つらくとも); 〜たい→たくとも; 〜ない→なくとも
examples: No matter how hard it gets, I won't give up until the end.
Even if I want to go, I can't because I have no money.

senses.label: Volitional + とも
senses.meaning: Whatever happens, however it goes, the result is unaffected. Often paired with 「誰が」, 「何と」 or 「たとえ」.
senses.connection: Verb volitional form／〜であろう + とも
examples: No matter what anyone says, my decision won't change.
Even if I fail, it's worth trying.

senses.label: At least / at the latest
senses.meaning: 「少なくとも」, 「遅くとも」, 「早くとも」 and 「多くとも」 are set adverbs meaning “at least”, “at the latest”, “at the earliest” and “at most”.
senses.connection: 少なく／遅く／早く／多く + とも
examples: I'll be back by five at the latest.
This job will take at least three days.

notes: Adjectives must take the ku-form: 「苦しくとも」 means “even if it hurts”; but 「苦しいとも」 would be the sentence-final particle “of course it hurts”, a different meaning.
「遅くとも」 and 「早くとも」 point in opposite directions: 「遅くとも五時に」 = by five at the latest (before five); 「早くとも五時に」 = not before five at the earliest (five or after).
Verbs take the volitional form: ✕「言ってとも」「言うとも」→ ○「何と言おうとも」.
The concessive 「とも」 is written-style; saying 「苦しくとも」 in conversation sounds affected, and people normally say 「苦しくても」.

daily.title: Reading a novel
daily.description: The hero confesses his feelings to his love.
daily.example: Even if the world ends, I'll be by your side.

daily.title: Setting a time
daily.description: Arranging when to meet a friend.
daily.example: I'll get there by seven at the latest.

daily.title: Cheering yourself on
daily.description: A line written in a diary.
daily.example: Even when it's hard, let's keep looking forward.

work.title: Business email
work.description: Replying to a client's inquiry.
work.example: We will contact you within next week at the latest.

work.title: Newspaper editorial
work.description: An editorial calls for reconstruction after a disaster.
work.example: Whatever difficulties there may be, we must complete the reconstruction.

etymology: 「とも」 is the particle 「と」 plus emphatic 「も」. In classical Japanese it was a conjunctive particle for concessive conditions (“even if”). Today it survives in written style and in set phrases like 「少なくとも」.

similar.title: 〜ても (even if)
similar.explanation: Same meaning. 「ても」 is the general form and attaches freely; 「とも」 is written-style and attaches only to the adjective ku-form, the verb volitional, etc.

similar.title: 〜(よ)うが／〜(よ)うと
similar.explanation: Same meaning as 「volitional＋とも」: both mean “no matter…”. 「ようと」「ようが」 are more common; 「ようとも」 is more literary and stronger.

similar.title: たとえ〜ても
similar.explanation: Both are concessive. 「たとえ〜ても」 is the general form; 「たとえ〜とも」 is more literary and solemn, and 「たとえ」 and 「とも」 often echo each other.

similar.title: 〜ずとも
similar.explanation: They share a source. 「ずとも」 is the form where 「とも」 follows the negative auxiliary 「ず」, meaning “even without…”.

formation: The particle 「とも」 is made of the case particle 「と」 plus 「も」, which marks concession or inclusion, and in classical Japanese it expresses a concessive condition, “even if…”. After the adjective ku-form it means “even in such a state”; after the verb volitional it means “even if it is going to happen like this”. 「も」 gives a concessive “even so” tone, so the main clause is always a result that remains unaffected. 「遅く＋とも」 literally means “even if late (not beyond this point)”, which has become the fixed limit expression “at the latest”; 「少なくとも」 and 「早くとも」 work the same way.

meaning: The written form of 「だろう」, expressing conjecture. Also used to modify nouns and in concessive or question forms.
connection: Noun／na-adjective stem + であろう; Verb／i-adjective plain form + であろう

senses.label: Written conjecture
senses.meaning: The speaker's guess, “probably ...”. More formal and weighty than 「だろう」. Common in papers, editorials and speeches.
senses.connection: Noun／na-adjective stem + であろう; Verb plain form + であろう
examples: This discovery will likely contribute greatly to the advancement of medicine.
It can probably be said that his judgment was correct.

senses.label: Modifying a noun
senses.meaning: 「〜であろう + noun」 means “... that will likely ...”, directly modifying a noun. 「だろう」 isn't normally used this way.
senses.connection: Verb dictionary form／ta-form + であろう + noun
examples: We need to discuss in advance the problems likely to arise in the future.
I want to answer a question that many people have probably wondered about.

senses.label: Concession / question
senses.meaning: 「〜であろうと（も）」 means “even if it is ...”. 「〜であろうか」 is a formal question or rhetorical question.
senses.connection: Noun + であろうと（も）／であろうか
examples: Even if you are a child, you must follow the rules.
Is this truly the right path?

notes: The na-adjective takes the stem: ✕「静かなであろう」→ ○「静かであろう」; nouns also attach directly: ○「事実であろう」.
「であろう」 belongs to the 「である」 style, so mixing it into a 「です・ます」 text or letter sounds inconsistent; use 「でしょう」 there.
Saying 「〜であろう」 to someone face to face sounds like a speech or talking down; in daily conversation use 「だろう」 or 「でしょう」.
「〜であろうと（も）」 is concessive “even if it's…”, not conjecture: 「子どもであろうと、ルールは守るべきだ」 = even a child should follow the rules.

daily.title: Reading an editorial
daily.description: An editorial predicts where a social issue is heading.
daily.example: This problem will likely become even more serious from now on.

daily.title: Watching a documentary
daily.description: The narrator describes how ancient people lived.
daily.example: It was probably here that they began a new life.

work.title: Writing a paper
work.description: Speculating in the conclusion about how widely the findings apply.
work.example: These results probably apply to other regions as well.

work.title: Graduation speech
work.description: The principal gives a speech at the ceremony.
work.example: Your hard work will surely be rewarded.

etymology: 「であろう」 comes from 「であら」 (the irrealis form of 「である」) plus the conjectural auxiliary 「う」 (classical 「む」). 「であらう」 changed in sound to 「であろう」. 「だろう」 is generally thought to be a contraction of 「であろう」.

similar.title: 〜だろう
similar.explanation: They share a source (「だろう」 is generally thought to be a contraction of 「であろう」) and mean the same. 「だろう」 is used in speech and ordinary writing; 「であろう」 is more formal and can modify nouns directly.

similar.title: 〜である
similar.explanation: They share a source. 「である」 is the written-style assertion “is”; 「であろう」 is its conjectural form, “probably is”.

similar.title: 〜ではなかろうか
similar.explanation: Both are written-style conjecture. 「ではなかろうか」 puts forth a claim gently in the form of a rhetorical question; 「であろう」 is a direct, general conjecture.

similar.title: 〜ものと思われる
similar.explanation: Both are written-style conjecture. 「ものと思われる」 softens subjectivity with the spontaneous form and is common in reports and news; 「であろう」 is the writer's direct inference, common in papers and editorials.

formation: This is the irrealis 「であら」 of 「である」 plus the conjectural auxiliary 「う」 (classical 「む」); 「であらう」 changed in sound to 「であろう」. 「である」 is the written-style assertion “is”, and adding the conjectural 「う」 turns it into “probably is”. Because it comes from 「である」, it naturally belongs to the written 「である」 style; and because the classical 「う（む）」 could modify nouns directly, it allows the attributive use seen in 「起こるであろう問題」, which 「だろう」 rarely allows. Adding 「と（も）」 makes it concessive, and adding 「か」 makes it a question or rhetorical question.
